title: The Jigsaw Classroom
text:
In 1971, schools in Austin, Texas, had just been desegregated, and classrooms that had been all white, all Black or all Hispanic suddenly mixed children who had never studied together. There was open hostility, and fights broke out. The school administration asked Elliot Aronson, then at the University of Texas, for help.

Aronson and his graduate students watched classrooms and concluded that the usual format made things worse: children competed for the teacher's attention and approval, and the weaker or newer students were often humiliated in front of the others.

They designed an alternative called the jigsaw classroom. Children were put into small, mixed groups of about five or six. The day's lesson, for example a biography, was divided into parts, and each child received only one part. Each child first met with members of other groups who had the same part to master it, then returned to teach it to their own group. The only way for anyone to learn the whole lesson was to listen to every member. Mocking a classmate meant losing their piece.

Compared with traditional classes, children in jigsaw classes came to like their groupmates more, including those of other ethnic groups, showed more self-esteem, and did as well or better on tests.
lesson: Make every member's knowledge essential to the shared goal. When people need each other's piece, they start to listen to and respect each other.
people: Elliot Aronson, Nancy Blaney, Cookie Stephan, Jev Sikes, Matthew Snapp
source: Aronson, E., Blaney, N., Stephan, C., Sikes, J., and Snapp, M. (1978). The Jigsaw Classroom. Sage Publications.
